---
title: "Overlap and Structure: The coverage strip"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

**Experimental.** This tutorial walks through `synthetic_coverage()`,
`gg_coverage()` and `blend_llms()`: Where synthetic respondents land compared
with real people (Overlap), and whether the items relate to each other as
they do in real people (Structure).

## Keyed data in the shape synthcheck expects

`synthetic_coverage()` works on the answers you give it, so key the
reverse-keyed items first. HEXACO answers run from 1 to 7, so a reverse-keyed
answer `x` becomes `8 - x`:

```{r}
library(synthcheck)

h <- hexaco_items$item[hexaco_items$trait == "H"]
rev_items <- intersect(h, hexaco_items$item[hexaco_items$reverse])
keyed <- function(d) { d <- d[h]; d[rev_items] <- 8 - d[rev_items]; d }

real <- keyed(hexaco_real[hexaco_real$country == "Canada", ])
ca <- hexaco_llm[hexaco_llm$country == "Canada" & hexaco_llm$attempt <= 4, ]
synthetic <- lapply(as_synthetic_list(ca), function(m) lapply(m, keyed))
str(synthetic, max.level = 1)
```

Each model has four attempts. An attempt is one full run of the personas, so
the spread over attempts shows how stable a model is.

## The coverage strip

```{r}
cov <- synthetic_coverage(synthetic, real, cor = "pearson")
cov
```

```{r, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 9}
gg_coverage(cov)
```

The columns are the deciles of the real total score, so each holds about 10%
of real people. A row is one model and attempt. Red cells hold fewer
synthetic respondents than real people, blue cells hold more, and pale cells
are a match within the noise of a real sample of the same size.

Here every model has a blue right end and a red left end: It piles its
respondents into the top deciles of Honesty-Humility, so its synthetic people
are more honest and humble than real Canadians. Gemma 4 26B spreads a little
further down the scale than the others.

**Overlap** sums, slice by slice, the smaller of the synthetic and the real
share. 100% is the same mix as the real data. **Structure** is 100% minus the
mean absolute difference between the real and synthetic inter-item
correlations.

`cor = "pearson"` is fast. With the polycor package installed, the default
`cor = "auto"` uses polychoric correlations, which suit 7-point items better
but take longer on many items.

## Other slices

`slices` changes what the columns are:

- `"score"` (the default): Deciles of the real total score.
- `"theta"`: Deciles of a unidimensional IRT score fitted to the real data.
- `"group"`: One column per group, such as a country or a persona.
- `"item"`: One column per answer category of each item, to see which
  categories a model avoids.

```{r, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 9}
cov_items <- synthetic_coverage(synthetic, real, slices = "item", cor = "pearson",
                                blend = FALSE)
gg_coverage(cov_items, items_per_plot = 8)
```

Items are ordered from the worst Item Overlap. Most models rarely use the low
categories that real people choose (red on the left of each item) and pile
their answers into one or two categories (blue).

With a grouping column, `within_group = TRUE` compares the shares within each
group, so that the mix of groups does not count. Use it when you set the
number of synthetic respondents per group by design.

## The best blend

With two or more models, `synthetic_coverage()` also searches for the mix of
models that matches real people best. `cov$blend` holds the recipe, and
`blend_llms()` searches again with other settings:

```{r}
cov$blend$recipe
b <- blend_llms(cov, step = 0.1, holdout = FALSE)
b$blend$weights
```

With four or more attempts per model, the recipe is chosen on half of the
attempts and reported on the other half, so the blend's numbers are not
flattered by the search.
